## Description

Euler's method is the simplest one-step numerical solver for an initial value problem $y' = f(t,y)$, $y(t_0)=y_0$, on $[t_0, b]$.
It computes $y_n \approx y(t_n)$ at the grid points $t_n = t_0 + nh$ of $m$ subintervals of width $h = (b - t_0)/m$, and advances the solution by following the local tangent at each grid point:

$$
y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(t_n,y_n), \qquad t_{n+1}=t_n+h.
$$

Mathews' modified Euler method is the explicit midpoint method: it takes a half Euler step to the middle of the step and uses the slope there,

$$
y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f\Bigl(t_n+\tfrac{h}{2},\ y_n+\tfrac{h}{2}f(t_n,y_n)\Bigr).
$$

Mathews' theorem for Euler's method assumes that $f$ is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in $y$, and his precision theorem that the solution is in $C^2[t_0, b]$.
Then, in general, the local truncation error is $O(h^2)$ and the global error is $O(h)$, so halving $h$ roughly halves the error.
For smooth enough $f$, modified Euler's global error is $O(h^2)$: halving $h$ divides it by about 4.

The animations use $y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}$, $y(0) = 1$ on $[0, 5]$, with $y(5) = 0.0081199$.
Here $f$ is not Lipschitz near $y = 0$, but the solution never falls below $y(5)$.
The table gives the largest grid-point error for the five finest $m$ that [Case 1](#case-1) and [Case 2](#case-2) share, with the observed order $p = \ln(E_{\text{prev}}/E)/\ln(m/m_{\text{prev}})$ against the row above.
It is about 1 for Euler and 2.1 to 2.3 for modified Euler, falling to 2.04 from $m = 300$ to $600$.

| $m$ | $h$ | Euler: largest error | $p$ | modified Euler: largest error | $p$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 80 | 0.0625 | $4.25 \times 10^{-2}$ | — | $6.27 \times 10^{-4}$ | — |
| 90 | 0.05556 | $3.77 \times 10^{-2}$ | 1.02 | $4.81 \times 10^{-4}$ | 2.26 |
| 100 | 0.05 | $3.39 \times 10^{-2}$ | 1.02 | $3.83 \times 10^{-4}$ | 2.16 |
| 120 | 0.04167 | $2.82 \times 10^{-2}$ | 1.01 | $2.56 \times 10^{-4}$ | 2.20 |
| 150 | 0.03333 | $2.25 \times 10^{-2}$ | 1.01 | $1.59 \times 10^{-4}$ | 2.14 |

The error at $t = 5$ alone misleads ([Case 1](#case-1), [Case 2](#case-2)): late in the run $\partial f/\partial y$ is strongly negative and damps the error made earlier.
At $m = 150$, Euler's error at $t = 5$ is $-1.7 \times 10^{-6}$ and modified Euler's $1.8 \times 10^{-6}$, although Euler's largest error is about 140 times larger.

In general, on $y' = \lambda y$, each step multiplies the error it inherits by $1 + z$ (Euler) or $1 + z + z^2/2$ (modified Euler), with $z = h\lambda$; for real $z < 0$ both have size at most 1 only for $-2 \le z \le 0$.
Here $\partial f/\partial y = -t/(3y^{2/3})$ reaches $-41.3$ at $t = 5$, so for $m \le 103$, $h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$ along the solution exceeds 2 before $t = 5$, the shaded region in the frames.
On the coarsest grids, Euler's runs for $m = 10$ to $40$ zig-zag and dip below zero although the solution stays positive ([Case 1](#case-1)), and modified Euler's runs zig-zag for $m = 12$ to $24$ and turn upward before $t = 5$ for $m = 28$ to $60$ ([Case 2](#case-2)).

[Heun's Method](../heuns-method/), which corrects an Euler predictor with the trapezoidal rule, is also of order 2; [Big "O" Truncation Error](../big-o-truncation-error/) explains the notation, the [Taylor Series Method](../taylor-series-method-for-odes/) and the [Runge-Kutta Method](../runge-kutta-method/) reach higher orders, the [Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg Method](../runge-kutta-fehlberg-method/) adapts the step size, and [Predictor-Corrector Methods](../predictor-corrector-methods/) such as [Adams-Bashforth-Moulton](../adams-bashforth-moulton-method/) use several previous points.

## Animations

Each animation below repeats one of Mathews' **step-refinement sweeps** for the IVP
$y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}$, $y(0)=1$ on $0 \le t \le 5$. Each frame is a complete run with
$m$ subintervals ($h=5/m$), for the values of $m$ in Mathews' animation, drawn over a gray
reference solution (fixed-step RK4 with 50 000 steps) and labelled with the computed $y(5)$,
its error at $t=5$ and the largest error at any grid point of the run. A light red band marks where $h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$, evaluated along the
reference solution rather than the plotted run, exceeds the method's stability limit.

Legacy archive note: Mathews' animations `Euleraa.gif` and `MEuleraa.gif` are in the
archive and sweep $m$ in the same way; every $y(5)$ printed in them agrees with the runs
here when rounded to seven decimals. The module's Examples 11 (Euler) and 12 (modified
Euler) each print runs with $m=40$, $100$ and $150$; their final values agree with this
page's frames for those $m$.

### Case 1 - Forward Euler step-refinement sweep, $y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}$, $y(0)=1$, $m = 10$ to $150$ subintervals {#case-1}

**Behavior:** The frames use the 20 values of Mathews' animation, $m = 10, 15, 20, 25, 30,
35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150$. The reference solution
rises from $y(0)=1$ to about $1.4498$ near $t=0.88$, then decays toward the nullcline
$y=1/t^3$ (where $y'=0$) and reaches $y(5)=0.0081199$. For $m=10$ to $40$ the computed
values zig-zag in the tail and dip below zero, although the exact solution stays positive;
they end at $y(5)\approx1.777$ for $m=10$, $0.391$ for $m=30$ and $-0.0174$ for $m=40$
(the first of the module's Example 11 runs, $m=40$, $100$ and $150$). At $m=45$ the last steps still alternate, but by less than
$0.009$, too little to see at this scale. From $m=50$ on the runs decrease steadily after
their peak, and the error at $t=5$ is small: $-4.2\times10^{-6}$ at $m=60$ and
$-1.7\times10^{-6}$ at $m=150$, where $y(5)\approx0.0081182$. It does not measure the
accuracy of the run: $\partial f/\partial y$ is strongly negative late in the run, which
damps the error made earlier, and from $m=55$ on the error at $t=5$ is more than $10^4$
times smaller than the largest error at any grid point ("max |error|" in each frame). For
$m=45$ to $150$ that largest error lies between $t=1.64$ and $1.73$, after the peak, where
the run is above the reference. It falls at every refinement in the sweep and, from $m=45$ on,
about halves when $m$ doubles, as expected of a first-order method: $5.7\times10^{-2}$ at $m=60$,
$2.8\times10^{-2}$ at $m=120$ and $2.2\times10^{-2}$ at $m=150$. The cause of the coarse-grid behaviour is stability:
$\partial f/\partial y=-t/(3y^{2/3})$ reaches $-41.3$ at $t=5$, so for steps longer than
about $h=0.0485$ ($m\le103$; here $m=10$ to $100$), $h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$ along the
reference solution exceeds Euler's stability limit $2$ before $t=5$ (the shaded region in
those frames). There, while the error is small compared with the reference solution, each
step multiplies the error it inherits by about $1+h\,\partial f/\partial y<-1$ and adds its
own local error, so the inherited part is amplified with alternating sign. For $m=10$ to
$40$ the error grows to more than $25$ times the reference solution at the same $t$, so
this linear picture no longer holds and individual steps can shrink the error: at $m=25$ the step from $t=4.2$
takes it from $+0.429$ to $-0.009$. At $m=10$ the onset is at $t\approx2.92$,
and for $m=10$ to $45$ the error at $t=5$ is larger than just before the onset. For $m=50$
to $100$ the onset comes later, from $t\approx3.95$ ($m=50$) to $t\approx4.95$ ($m=100$),
and the amplified part stays too small to see: these runs decrease steadily, and their error
at $t=5$ is smaller than just before the onset. For $m=110$ to $150$,
$h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$ stays below $2$ up to $t=5$.

For m = 10 to 40 the run zig-zags in the tail and dips below zero, ending at y(5) = 1.777 for m = 10; for m = 10 to 100 a shaded region marks where h·|∂f/∂y|, evaluated on the reference solution, exceeds 2; from m = 50 on the run decreases steadily after its peak, with y(5) = 0.0081182 at m = 150. ### Case 2 - Modified Euler (midpoint) step-refinement sweep, same IVP, $m = 12$ to $150$ subintervals {#case-2}

**Behavior:** The frames use the 21 values of Mathews' animation, $m = 12, 14, 16, 18, 20,
24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 120, 150$, and the same reference
solution as Case 1. For $m=12$ to $24$ the tail zig-zags; at $m=24$ only the last three steps
alternate ($+0.069$, $-0.076$, $+0.489$), ending at $y(5)\approx0.613$. For $m=28$ to $60$
the curve turns upward before $t=5$ instead of following the decay (at $m=28$ with one small
dip of $0.0075$ in the second-to-last step), rising from its minimum by $0.35$ at $m=28$,
$0.057$ at $m=40$ and $0.015$ at $m=60$ (barely visible at this scale) and ending at
$y(5)\approx0.384$, $0.0761$ (the first of the module's Example 12 runs, $m=40$, $100$ and $150$) and $0.0259$. At $m=70$ the upturn
is only $0.0008$, too small to see, and from $m=80$ on the runs decrease steadily after
their peak. From $m=16$ the error at $t=5$ falls at every refinement in the sweep, to
$2.5\times10^{-4}$ at $m=80$ and $1.8\times10^{-6}$ at $m=150$, where
$y(5)\approx0.0081217$. For $m=16$ to $70$ it is also the largest error of the run, but from
$m=80$ on the same damping as in Case 1 makes it $2.5$ to $87$ times smaller than the largest error, which
lies between $t=3.19$ and $3.22$: $6.3\times10^{-4}$ at $m=80$ and $1.6\times10^{-4}$ at
$m=150$. From $m=80$ to $150$ that largest error falls by a factor of $3.9$, close to the
$(150/80)^2\approx3.5$ of a second-order method, while Euler's falls by $1.9$, close to
$150/80\approx1.9$. At $m=150$ it is about 140 times smaller than Euler's
$2.2\times10^{-2}$, although the two errors at $t=5$ are about the same size. The method's amplification factor $1+z+z^2/2$, with
$z=h\,\partial f/\partial y$, has size at most 1 on the negative real axis exactly for
$-2\le z\le0$, so its stability limit is $2$, the same as Euler's: for $m\le103$ (here
$m=12$ to $100$), $h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$ along the reference solution exceeds $2$
before $t=5$ (the shaded region), from $t\approx2.99$ at $m=12$ to $t\approx4.95$ at $m=100$, and for each of these
$m$ the error at $t=5$ is larger than just before the onset. For $m=120$ and $150$,
$h\,|\partial f/\partial y|$ stays below $2$ up to $t=5$.
